samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Bert Cowan was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran, Bert Cowan. Mr. Cowan served in the U.S. Army with the 70th Division, 275th Regiment, Company A. He served in the European theater, and his highest rank was PFC. I'm Tom Swope and this recording was made at Mr. Cowan's home in Shaker Heights, Ohio on June 26th, 2001. Bert was 77 at the time of this recording. - - - -

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When did you go into the service?

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: I went into the service February of 1943 and was discharged in February of 1946. I was overseas for 13 months in Europe. We landed in Marseille and then we moved right up. As soon as we got there, we were on the front lines, and we were on the front lines for over 90 days straight. We were just below of where the breakthrough was at the Battle of the ___. They brought us up to fill in the holes there, and we caught a lot of German tanks and fire in that area, more so than I knew about after I read about what we went through, because you really couldn't tell. You know, you were by yourself. I was with the company headquarters of my outfit. I carried a 300M radio on my back, and then also we strung wire when we drew outposts and various other things to keep the communications going. And then, you know, we went through the war. I was wounded with -- from a tank that was shooting at us and this is -- this is the story about it. You can read about it, because unfortunately I'm a very -- I'm a cynic about the leadership that we had over there. And in looking back, none of these people knew what they were doing, and unfortunately, they caused a lot of people to die because of not knowing, okay. I don't think anybody wanted anybody else killed, but a lot of the officers there really didn't know what they were doing, and this was -- you read that story, you'll find out about one of 'em. And we went through the war. Fortunately, I was wounded but not very bad and finished out the war. We took -- we were -- occupied Frankfort. We came in and we stayed there, the occupation force, then were relieved -- they put us in a little town, a village outside of Frankfort. And then we had nothing to do. We played baseball, and it was this little stream and we would swim there. And, you know, I mean, the war was over. We were waiting to see what was going to happen with Japan, whether we were going to be shipped over there or not. And then they broke up the division and we went to the third division and I checked in there. And then they had a sign, anybody want to play football, so I signed up to play football, and I spent about five -- four or five months. We traveled all over Europe. We played in Berlin, in Paris and Manheim and various other places in Germany. And that was pretty good because there was no army involved in it. We had officers and everybody was equal, and it's the -- going back. I went into the Army and I was at Fort Lewis, Washington in the infantry, and I had signed up to go to the air corps, and it was awful. I hated it. I was in top physical condition. I had worked in a defense plant after getting out of high school, and then I was in college. I played college football for one year. I went to Mount Union College, and there wasn't an ounce of fat on me, and I got soft in the Army. We were in Fort Lewis, and then they were going on Louisiana maneuvers, and I decided I don't want to go on these Louisiana maneuvers, and I contacted the Air Force at Mather Field up in Washington, and I was able to take a test there {coughing} and the commanding officer said nobody could go to the air corps. Well, I got -- well, how it happened was that in my outfit -- and there was prejudice. I'm Jewish, and there was prejudice in there. I was originally with the 44th Division, which is New York National Guard, and a lot of guys from New York City, you know, tough guys, you know, the company commander there -- or the captain. And I had just recently come back from holiday with -- from Jewish holiday and then I came in and one of my friend's mother and father were coming into Seattle to visit him. So I came into the office, and it was a little Irish guy that was the first sergeant. And I said Patty, I'd like a weekend pass because my aunt and uncle are coming in. He walks into the CO's office there and he says, you know, tells him what happened. He says that fucking Jew, he said, wants another pass. Patty walks out and he's red. He said I want a transfer. I got a transfer the next day into the medical corps where my buddy was in. Because I was in the medical corps, their company commander was a major, he signed all my papers, he didn't care. So I got out of that, and I went to -- down to Texas -- to Amarillo, Texas to take some tests. And I think there was 80 or 90 of us from our division, and I think about 10 of us passed, and they were all privates. They were first sergeants and everything else, went up to Mather Field, California and were waiting to go to preflight. And that was beautiful, you know, it was great getting an air corps thing. They had bowling alleys and swimming pools and, you know, from where we were and to come there. And then one day they call us out -- all out, and they said well, we got orders that all -- everybody who came from the ground forces had to go back. Well, then we were shipped up to the 70th Division up at Camp Adair, Oregon. Our division, the 70th division, was mostly comprised of air corps cadets and ASTP, if you know what that was. That was -- ASTP, they sent certain armed forces to college. Why, I don't know, but they sent them there to study. They brought all these back. Our outfit had the highest IQ of any division in the country. And we had some fun with some of the noncoms who were there, because they weren't as smart as we were and we had 'em going pretty good. Anyway, we spent time in Oregon. Let's see, I was in Washington for almost a year and then in Oregon, we were there about four months, five months. And then we went to saint -- Missouri, Fort Leonard Wood, and then we did some more training there. And then we went to Boston and then we shipped out in December. We got a huge -- our whole division was down there, about 15,000 people were on that boat. We landed in Marseille and they told us don't go in -- don't go into Marseille by yourself 'cause the Berbers were there with the big swords, okay, and they'll kill ya. So we were very careful. We went in in twos and threes into Marseille.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Why?

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: And --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Why would they kill you?

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: Why not, okay? I mean, this was from the African, you know -- anyway, nobody really got hurt, but they camped us out in these tents up in the -- it was rainy and muddy, and finally they pulled us outta there, and we took 40 and 8 trains and we took some trucks, and they brought us up to the -- oh, it was like an old factory. And we were -- everybody got there and this buddy of mine, there was two of us together and you sleep on a floor, you put one blanket down and another one on top of you and you're so -- and we're in the middle of sleeping and all of a sudden this guy, I felt a kick. This captain of the battalion intelligence kicking me -- or not -- no, it wasn't intelligence. He was with communications. He kicked me and I jumped up, and I said don't you ever kick me again or, I said, you'll never live to talk about. He says you're talking to me like a civilian. I says you're fucking well right I'm talking to you like a civilian. Well, he and I got -- we had been -- we had a long-standing battle. In fact, he stopped me from elevating to sergeant and so forth. And then we moved up to the front lines. And the first -- I mean, combat, we're coming up this road and all of a sudden they start firing and we jump in the ditch and it's wet and you've got to go, you know, get up to go. Okay. You go in there, and that's what happened. And then, you know, we got through that. And then we moved up. Oh, sometime later on, we were marching down this -- through this village down like this and up a hill, and I was with the company commander and my captain in the front. And we come up and we turned around and we see these Tiger tanks coming down. Well, I didn't wait. I turned around and hightailed it. Now, part of us got away and half of the company was captured. And one of the guys who was captured was a very close friend of mine who -- he and I had been together for -- since we were there. In fact, an anecdote about it, when we were in Boston, we were out one night and we knew we were leaving, so we bought a pint of whiskey. And we said when the war's over, we'll celebrate. Well, I carried that thing in my gas mask, and then I put it in my duffel bag, and I carried it until the end of the war and then pulled it out and the first drink I threw away for him. He was captured during that period. I took off with a lot of other fellows. We were out there for, I don't know, 48 hours without food or water, drinking out of streams. I got dysentery from that -- and that's another story -- and I was, you know, three different pants and it was going. Anyway, we got back to our outfit and they brought in recruits and so forth. And then the second in command became the company commander. He was a lieutenant, a snot-nosed guy. Anyway we were -- they put us -- we relieved an outfit on the side of a hill, and it was so goddamned cold you couldn't -- you couldn't stand. You couldn't lie down. You try to dig a foxhole, you can't dig a foxhole 'cause it's ice. We -- you had to jump up and down to keep warm. And we did build a little foxhole, and then we got word to move out. And this lieutenant was sitting in this foxhole crying, and I had to direct the company out of that outfit -- to get out, you know, why each -- A company, B company and C company to get out of there, or the squads really. It wasn't the company, it was the squads. We got outta there. And then, this is -- you can read this 'cause this'll tell you one of the other things that -- that happened. Another thing was we had laid wire to all of our outposts, and all of a sudden -- and we had set up a telephone so that you could ring and, you know, we ring and we don't hear anything. Pitch black out. {laughing} Now you've got to follow the wire to find out where -- what's happening, what happened to 'em. Well, the captain said you get out there, and so we pick up the wire and we follow and we get over there and these guys are asleep, {laughing} and they unhooked the telephone. So the lieutenant's with 'em and I just raised holy hell. I said you got me out here, you coulda got me killed. Hook that thing up. Okay. And there was -- you know, sometimes we went out on patrol. They expected us to go into, you know, go out and find out and go in a German village. Nonsense, okay. We weren't -- weren't that stupid that we were going to risk our lives. We get down to the bottom of the hill, and all of a sudden somebody said wait, hold it. Okay, now, that was us, it wasn't a lot of 'em. We had one fella that went out by himself into the German territory and brought home prisoners. I don't -- forget his name. I think he was a Mexican kid from down in Texas or someplace, but he would go out by himself and bring back prisoners or get information of what was happening. And we ended up overlooking the Zigfried Line, and then we moved out of there. And I told you about the dysentery, and we -- they had to stop an attack because I had to stop and go, okay. {laughing} Well, it wasn't really attack, it was a march. And finally we got in Frankfort, and we didn't have any really basic resistance there. But we were under fire -- artillery fire quite a bit, not really hand-to-hand fire, and -- or hand-to-hand combat with the Germans. We -- they surrendered. And thank goodness it wasn't in Japan, I mean, you know, in the -- in the -- it was a different war than it was in the Orient, because you had to kill 'em. They didn't know what it meant to surrender. And we were in towards the end, and fortunately, I came through unscathed, except for a little wound, and, you know, as I look back on it, I was -- I had gone to college, and I had to go -- leave college to go to the service and I never went back to college, but it took three years out of my life that, you know, I could have used to much better advantage.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What happened to your buddy that was captured?

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: He -- I saw him twice. He lived through it. And first time I saw him was in California. He lived in -- he was a violinist with the MGM Symphony, and they put him in the infantry {laughing}. Okay. And I saw him. I was out there. I belonged -- was with the Men's of Pearl Club (ph.) of Ohio and I was a president. And we had a convention out there. And I went out there and I met him. I saw him and his wife and daughter and son. And then he had a business and he was out here on business, and he was in Akron and I spent an evening with him. And then, you know, I didn't pay -- lost track, together we hadn't done anything and then I had -- once I joined the 70th division, I found out that he had died the previous year. So I never did get a chance to see him, but there's some other fellas that, you know, I was close with that, and when I went to the reunion, none of the people that I really knew were there. I had called a few people that I got their addresses and so forth and called them and talked with them and -- to make sure that I had the right information on the article that I wrote for the magazine, and that's about it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you have any particular memories of anything with your buddy or buddies before he was captured while you were over there?

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: While we were over there?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any --

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: It happened so fast.

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: No, no, he was -- no, he was with -- in a -- he wasn't in the same area with me, I mean, he was in a company -- I mean in a squad.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: And we weren't -- we weren't together. You know, we saw each other, but, no, I mean, of the fellas that -- well, we played baseball after the war when we were in these little towns. Our Italian -- we had baseball teams, so we used to play baseball, but never -- never, unfortunately, kept contact with anybody. There was a couple fellas I'm trying to find. Whether they're still living or not, I don't know. Who -- well, there was a lot of experiences that we had even over there, but I haven't -- I confiscated a motorcycle -- motor bike, rather. And then from this little town, I would go into Frankfort or we would go in -- yeah, and spend the night there. They always had good food there. They had like a -- like a station where trucks would come in and they served food 24 hours a day, and we'd go there and eat and spend a weekend in Frankfort or something but I had that bike that I used. And I remember -- well, a lot of memories. The one thing that was most disgusting that -- we had a company commander, unfortunately, from Oklahoma. And I don't -- when I say this, there's no malice when I say it, but he carried a Bible with him which he read all the time. And the most humiliating thing that we went through was that some woman in Frankfort accused one of our guys of raping her. And this SOB threw the whole company out and let her walk around and pick him out. To me that was the most humiliating thing. I was just furious about it. Nothing you could do. You going to take her word for it? This is an enemy, okay. And they picked -- she picked some guy up and they got him court martialled, and these are guys who fought with him.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How were the people when you were occupying Germany in general?

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: There was no Nazis there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-hmm.

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: People next door weren't Nazis, not me, okay, that's what it was like. That's what it was like. You couldn't find any Nazis.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But you didn't have much contact with the local people really?

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: Well, I did with one man who said he was Jewish and he had a daughter, and we did have contact with him. But, you know, after we moved out of there, never after that. I don't know whether he was or not. At least he said he was. You had no way of knowing. No, we weren't allowed -- remember, you weren't allowed to fraternize that they knew about.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: {Laughing} Anybody getting away with anything they didn't know about?

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: Yeah, oh, sure.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What kinds of things?

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: Well, guys had women there, you know. You weren't supposed to fraternize with anybody, but that happened.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Backtracking, do you remember any specific pranks that you pulled on the cadets?

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: Any what?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: The pranks you were talking about pulling on the cadets during training, having fun with the --

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: Well, you mean -- not the cadets --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: The ASTP --

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: No, with the noncoms.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: We would sit there and we'd sit there like this, and they got irate 'cause you weren't paying attention, and they ask you a question and we'd answer it, okay. {laughing} And I once said to them, you know, we don't have to look at you to hear you and know what you're saying. I mean, we -- well, I had learned -- I'd been in the Army long enough to goof off whenever I could. And when we got up to Oregon, the first sergeant was a nice guy and he liked me. And I got out of the 25-mile hikes and a lot of other stuff. I spent the day sleeping like a sad sack. But I guess it was what you knew and who you knew. It's like anything else. And some of the fellas did better than others and others didn't. We lost a lot of men in our combat. I mean, the one thing that I remember -- in this article that I wrote where a fellow standing next to me was shot through the head, and we'd lost a lot of replacements there, wounded and trench feet and sickness and so forth.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was your hometown during the war?

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: Yeah, I went to Shaw High. I graduated in 1942, and I've lived here all my life.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember getting letters when you were overseas, anything, letters or packages?

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: Yeah. My folks used to send me packages. What they did, they send me cherries, but they took the juice out and they put liquor in there {laughing}, and I -- that and salamis, yeah. But I used to get that all the time in big packages, but they had that all figured out. You can get drunk on the cherries.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And you didn't share those with anybody else?

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: Oh, yeah, everybody got pack -- after the war, everybody got, you know, when we were in Frankfort and other places, we'd get packages. And then we used to get -- I don't know where we got the sardines and we got Rye bread, and we used to have a party at night late at night. We'd have -- eat stuff, you know -- well, after the war was over, it was easy, it wasn't that tough.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember where were you when VE Day came?

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: Yeah, we were in Frankfort.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any celebrations?

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: Yeah, we got drunk. I had that pint of whiskey. We got drunk that night, sure, but there were still -- you know, the guys were still fighting. What happened is we came in to Frankfort, and Patton spread out like this and we couldn't catch up again to the front. He was moving too fast, and so they kept us there in occupation forces. Then they moved us out when they brought in ___. The headquarters came into Frankfort at the ___+___, that complex.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You were talking about the leaders that had some disregard for their soldiers, did you think that Patton was like this?

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: Oh, Patton was blood and guts, your blood and his guts, but he got the job done. He saved lives by doing it. That wasn't what I was talking about. There were some others --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: He had the respect of the men over there?

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: Yeah, yeah. We saw Patton one day. We were coming back from Paris playing football in Frankfort and we were in a train station, and he come up with that shiny helmet and that white coat with the stripes. And he came up, where you guys going? We just came back from playing football. He says how did you do? We lost. He said oh, that's too bad, and walked away. Very impressive figure, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: The football team, would you go and travel and play a team that was in that area then?

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: Yeah, sure, we played a team in Paris.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And they had a team ready for you to play and --

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: Oh, everybody had a team. We --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You got to travel all over there?

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: Yeah. What was it? Was it the hundred and -- what was the -- we played one of the air -- one of the -- hundred and second division or something in Berlin, you know, the Berlin Stadium. Yeah, we played different div -- every division that were still there had a team. So we had our own little town. We had our own football field and mess hall and everything. We played Hearts all day long when we weren't -- we weren't -- we weren't practicing. But that was good times.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was there any entertainment that you remember when you were over there?

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: No, we never saw the Red Cross. They never come up as far as we were close. Only time I saw the Red Cross -- Red Cross was in Paris where we went into the officers' club there. That's where we saw the Red Cross. They didn't -- they never came -- not too close to the front.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Bob Hope didn't bring his USO show anywhere close to you?

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: No, we saw one USO show. I think I have it down. I don't remember who it was, Frances Langford -- no, I'm not sure who was -- that was. We did see one, that was all.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And that was after the war was over?

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: Yeah. Not only -- we'd rather have a bath than see a show. I don't know how long we went before we got showers and clean clothes. That was quite a day when they brought us back for showers and changing clothes. But I had dysentery for a long time. I had three layers of clothes, and part of 'em were hanging up, you know, couldn't stop it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So when did you come back?

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: I came back in February of '46 on a victory ship that came out of Bramerhaven. We went through the Eden's Channel in February, and I didn't get out of that -- out of my bunk I think for four days until we got into the, what do they call it, the southern -- what do they call that, when you get out of the channel and then you go into the warm water? Well, and then it was very nice. I think it took us, I don't know, ten days to get back. And then we landed at Fort Dix and then we went to Indiantown Gap and then I was discharged from Indiantown Gap.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any particular memories about coming home that ___+___ --

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: Yeah. We have nice crap games, card games. I won a new car. Well, In those days cars weren't expensive.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-hmm.

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: But yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You won that on the trip over -- back home?

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How did you collect on the car?

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: Hmm?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How did you collect on that car?

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: How did I collect it?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did the person deliver the car to you {laughing}?

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: Oh, no, no, no -- I won the money shooting crap --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You just won that money ___ --

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: -- and playing poker, yeah, when I got home. We played in Berlin and we went into the Russian section and I had ten cartons of cigarettes. I didn't smoke cigarettes, I smoked cigars. And within five minutes, I was getting a hundred dollars a carton. I had a thousand dollars in scrip money, 'cause Russians had the same kind of money we had did. Now, we went to Paris the following week, and I think we spent something like five hundred. Couldn't get the money home. I remember once going to -- 'cause you couldn't wire your money home, but you could buy flowers. So I went there for, I don't know, Mother's Day or whatever it was, and I sent everybody I knew in the United States flowers. And then I saw -- we met an officer at the Folies Bergere, and we were talking. He's going home. So I said jeez, can you get this money home for me? I don't know, and I gave him two hundred, three hundred dollars, and he did, he got it home for me. But everything was great. Guys were selling tanks to the Russians. I read about that, tanks, whatever they could sell, jeeps, I mean, they're going to get them back, but the Russians had the same kind of money as we did, and they didn't know what to do with it, didn't know what it was. So they were selling everything, watches. Yeah, guys came back -- some fellas came back with a lot of money.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were there a lot of souvenir collectors in your unit?

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: No, not really. When you mean souvenir, like --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You know, enemy war souvenirs.

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: Well, no. We collected -- you know, if there were bodies, we went through them to see what they had. Watches, I had a whole armful of watches at one time, but -- and marks, but the marks didn't mean anything, you know. You didn't get -- yeah, some of 'em got the Lugers -- the German Lugers, which was a prize if you got an officer, but the -- their infantrymen didn't have anything, I mean, they had guns, but nobody wanted 'em. We didn't need 'em.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Anything come to mind as your most vivid memory of that whole experience?

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: Well, I can read you this.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Go ahead and tell me this so we have it on tape.

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: Well, we started off on a -- a midnight trek to capture a building on the top of a -- like a bluff, and we had -- we didn't have our regular officer. We had the captain from battalion intelligence who had never led an attack before, and we had to go down a big valley, I mean a wooded -- very tough terrain and go back up. And he moved so fast that he lost half the company. We finally got to the top. We saw the building and pulled over on the side, and he said dig in. And I was with him. I was carrying the radio. And there's a tank sitting right by the building. Okay. This is late at night, and in my mind, I said you're going to dig in, they're gonna know we're here. The lights were on in the building, you know, they knew -- I said let's attack the building now. I didn't say it in that way. I said wouldn't it be a good idea to attack that building now? No, no, no, we're going to do it in the morning. He says everybody dig in. Now you could hear the shovels and everything else going. Then he sets up guards every two hours or every hour, and we're supposed to get up at, you know, 5:00 and attack at 5:00. I wake up and I see the sun shining, beautiful day. And I look over and I see that turret of the tank moving towards us, and it gives a burst. I got hit. I dove over him and I took off and I ran. And I was the only one I think that -- from this thing. From what I found out, anybody there was captured. I was the only one who got out, you know, not -- it's not that you could stay and fight, okay. This was stupidity and I wasn't stupid. So I took off and I ran. And as I'm running, they had trenches coming back, and I'm running down and I see these Germans in the trenches and I'm firing at them. And I finally get back to the -- to our -- and I don't know what happened up there. But I finally get back to our company headquarters and the first sergeant, I said I'm not going back. I said I've had it, forget it, I'm not going to go back there and get killed for no reason. He said slow down, go to the first aid station, take care of your wound. So I went back to the first aid station and took care of my wound, and that's how I got the Purple Heart. Next day, there's a -- we got to go back up and get 'em. So we go back up, but we didn't go that way. We went through a road. And it was daylight, and we started to attack, and there was like a big tree had fallen in front with a huge stump -- not stump, you know where it comes out?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uhm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: And the captain is there, and I'm there and our B-A-R man is there. You know what a B-A-R --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: He carried it. All right. And we're firing. The rest of the troops are behind us, 'cause we had ___, and first thing I know is he gets shot right through the head. Captain's got a pistol and he says pistol doesn't work. He says give me your carbine. I give him my carbine. I'm on the radio trying to get some artillery fire. I look around, he's gone. He took off and left me there. Well, I finally got ahold of our artillery and started to direct traffic. Well, the first shots hit into our -- where we were. Now, it was a little difficult because I was here and they were here. Okay. It's not firing over our head, it's firing over here. Well, finally, I -- and I had never done that before, you know, directing artillery fire, but when they fired in and said the shells are landing here, I said go to your right, go to your right. And finally, they zeroed in and they led a blast and finally we went there and they had killed most of the Germans, and they were dug in the trenches on that side, nothing on the other side that was where we came up. So finally, we took that building and we stayed there for quite awhile until we moved out to take Saarbrücken, but that was it. Here's -- when I said that the captain, in all due respect, shouldn't have been leading that, because we should have gone in that night and taken it and captured it. Would have saved a lot of lives, and I know there's some, but people got killed up there and most of them were captured, because I talked to a few that were there on that particular event, you know. That was one of 'em. Another one, when I mentioned to you about this lieutenant where -- who was crying in a foxhole, had to lead an attack on a building that was in a valley that had Germans in it. You know, it was supposed to be an early dawn attack. Well, he didn't -- he waited at the bottom of the hill until it got light and then took off, and guys -- so many people killed in that thing. And well, I met one of the fellas at one of the meetings. He lost a leg there. But, I mean, just ridiculous. If he had gone out early in the morning in the darkness, they could have taken the building and nothing would have happened because we had -- we were the superior -- I mean, these guys were there. The Germans were there, but that was easy to fight when you saw somebody and nobody was shooting at you. Those were the few things that I remember where officers wasted lives.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You think it was fear or lack of training?

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: Fear.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Fear?

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: No, it was fear with him. Sure, it was fear. It wasn't lack of training. It was fear. And he shouldn't have been where he was. Now, this happened quite a bit. The best officers came -- were the ones that were made officers right on the battlefield. These were soldiers who had fought. They knew what they were doing. Okay. They weren't 90 day wonders, okay, which you read about. Not all of 'em were bad. I can't say that every one was bad or didn't know what they were doing, but most of the battlefield commission -- fellas who had battlefield commissions knew what they were doing and knew how to protect their men and so forth. What else can I tell you, Tom?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any trouble adjusting to civilian life after --

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- the stint?

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: Yes. I had such an inferiority complex that if I went in a restaurant, I felt everybody was watching me. If I dropped a fork, just awful. Well, I knew what it was and it took -- I had to -- I fought it, because I was in sales. Okay. So fortunately, I knew what it was and it took awhile before I had beat it. It was -- it was tough.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So what exactly did -- where did that inferiority complex come from you think?

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: Well, I -- I don't know whether it's inferiority complex as much as the whole world's watching me.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Just self-conscious because --

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: Yeah, self-consciousness, yes, not inferiority, self-consciousness. I don't think I was ever had an inferiority complex.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Because you felt different from all the people --

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: Well, I can't explain why.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: It was just being out of touch with the civilian population for three years.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And did a lot of what was going on around you when you came back seem kind of trivial after what you'd been through?

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: Well, no, I don't think it had to do with the people there, because most of my close friends came back too and so we hung out together. But when I was with them, everything was fine, but when I was by myself and I was traveling and I had to, you know, go to restaurants and stuff like that, it was like -- like this, that everybody was watching me. But I was fortunate enough to know or to realize what the problem was and to work on it, work on it, to fight it. And I didn't have any medical help to do it. Fortunately, I got through it all right.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That sounds similar. I've heard of other guys talk about anxiety attacks that they would have after --

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: No, I never had an anxiety attack.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: It wasn't -- it didn't go to that extreme?

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: It was just a --

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: Just go like this.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: You know, you're eating, all of a sudden you drop a fork, oh my God. So I took up drinking {laughter}.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: There you go. That will solve it, that will calm your nerves.

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: No, no, by that time -- when I started drinking, I didn't have any attacks anymore, I mean, I didn't -- that wasn't one of my problems.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: The attacks stopped before the drinking?

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: Yeah -- no, this happened -- I don't think I would drink. I don't remember during that period of -- I've never been a heavy drinker, a social drinker. And when I was single and dating, we'd go out and we'd drink pretty good, okay.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you have a girlfriend during the war?

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: Not really. I got a lot of Dear John letters.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: {Laughter} You got a lot of Dear John letters?

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: No. One -- one, but it was all right. I wasn't --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Why did she want to break up?

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: Well, it wasn't that. It wasn't an ongoing thing. It wasn't a serious well, we're going to get married and everything else. We had just been dating, and I left and she kept writing me. And then, you know, she found somebody else. It's all right. Didn't break my heart. Broke my heart when my best friend was in the Navy and he was writing me from Hawaii. He was on duty in Hawaii as an enson.{laughter}

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Kind of broke your heart?

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: Yeah, and I'm in a foxhole {laughter}.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: {Laughter} This would be after Pearl Harbor, though, right?

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: Yeah, yeah, sure. We went in after Pearl Harbor, but I'd get letters from him and I'd write him back, you son of a --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: {Laughter} And that's where he was stationed the whole time --

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: He didn't have to --

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: Nope.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Tough job?

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: Oh, yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Anything else you can think of, does that cover it?

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: That just about covers it, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Is this a copy or is this --

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, I can take this?

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: Yeah, you can take that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Great. Where was this published?

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: In our 70th Division. It's not like a newspaper. It's a booklet they send out twice -- three times a year. You had some tough times and you had some good times.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right ___, yeah.

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: You were young and --

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: You didn't know that much, but --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: It was --

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: But you -- you had a spirit that you were doing something for the country.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: And it was a war that we went in to win, not like Vietnam.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Not like Vietnam, when we went into a defensive war and --

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: No, it was a war we went in not to win, that's all.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Exactly.

sp.speaker: Bert Cowan
sp.p: It wasn't defense. They went in not to win.
[End of interview]
